blocks.title: Key ideas
blocks.md: **Post-colonial criticism** studies how literature deals with colonialism and its after-effects. Key ideas: **centre and margin**; the colonised as the **‘Other’** in colonial writing (discussed by Edward Said); **hybridity**, the mixing of cultures (Homi Bhabha); **language and power**; **resistance** and **writing back**, where writers answer colonial representations; and **decolonising** the canon.

blocks.title: Applying the approach
blocks.md: Ask: Who speaks and who is silent? How are places and peoples described? What does language choice imply? How does the text show cultural mixing, loss or resistance? Does the text accept or challenge colonial stereotypes? Always ground the reading in specific words.

items.text: How are people and places described?

blocks.caption: Questions to ask in a post-colonial reading.
blocks.alt: Four boxes: voice, description, language and resistance or hybridity.

blocks.title: Strengths and limits
blocks.md: **Strengths:** highlights power and history; makes visible silenced voices. **Limits:** may reduce a text to politics; ‘post-colonial’ covers very different regions and experiences; must avoid ignoring aesthetic qualities, individual authors and non-political themes.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.md:
- Applying theory without evidence from the text.
- Treating all colonised societies as the same.
- Assuming a text has only one political meaning.
- Misusing terms: ‘hybridity’ is not simply ‘mixture’ but a creative blending with power implications.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Apply the ‘Other’
blocks.statement: Original passage from an imaginary traveller’s diary: ‘The villagers were strange and silent, a part of the landscape, like the trees. They did not seem to have thoughts of their own.’ Analyse using post-colonial ideas.
steps: The traveller treats the villagers as an ‘Other’, part of the landscape.
The comparison with trees denies individuality.
The diary assumes a colonial viewpoint and silences their voices; a post-colonial reading would expose this bias.
blocks.answer: A colonial gaze presenting people as an object and ‘Other’.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Writing back
blocks.statement: Original: a poem titled ‘Reply to the Diary’ gives the villagers’ own names, voices and humour. How does it ‘write back’?
steps: It challenges the earlier silence and stereotype.
Naming gives individuality.
Humour and voice reclaim narrative control.
blocks.answer: It counters stereotypes by giving voice and names.

blocks.title: Feminist criticism
blocks.md: **Feminist criticism** examines how literature represents **gender**, how women and men are shown, whose voice is heard, and how **patriarchy** (male dominance) shapes the text and its reception. It asks about stereotypes, silence, agency and whether the text reinforces or challenges gender roles. Writers often cited include Virginia Woolf and Simone de Beauvoir for general ideas.

blocks.title: Formalism
blocks.md: **Formalism** (including New Criticism) focuses on the **text itself**: form, structure, language, imagery, irony and ambiguity, and how they work together. Biography and history are secondary. The method is **close reading**: a careful analysis of how the words create meaning.

items.text: How do form and words work?

blocks.caption: Four critical lenses and their questions.
blocks.alt: A table with four critical lenses and the key question of each.

blocks.title: Other lenses
blocks.md: **Reader-response** studies how readers create meaning. **Marxist** criticism examines class and economic power. **Historical or biographical** approaches look at context. Different approaches highlight different features, and a strong essay may combine them while staying focused on the text.

blocks.title: Avoid
blocks.md:
- Using theory as a label rather than as a method with evidence.
- Assuming feminist criticism is only about women characters: it also considers masculinity and language.
- Treating formalism as ‘ignoring meaning’: it seeks meaning through form.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Feminist reading
blocks.statement: Original passage: ‘Maria served the guests without sitting. The men’s voices rose around her; she was asked for more water, and no one asked her opinion.’ Give a feminist reading.
steps: Maria works while others talk: a gendered division of tasks.
‘No one asked her opinion’ shows silence and lack of agency.
The passage may highlight the unequal voices in the household.
blocks.answer: It exposes inequality of voice and labour.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Formalist reading
blocks.statement: Use the same passage for a formalist reading.
steps: Form: simple sentences and repetition of serving actions create a steady rhythm.
The contrast between ‘voices rose’ and her silence is built through juxtaposition.
The structure mirrors her position at the edge of the conversation.
blocks.answer: Rhythm, contrast and structure convey her marginal position.

blocks.title: Irony and satire
blocks.md: **Verbal irony** says the opposite of what is meant; **situational irony** is an outcome contrary to expectation; **dramatic irony** is when the audience knows more than the characters. **Satire** uses humour, exaggeration and irony to criticise society, institutions or behaviour, often hoping to reform them. **Parody** imitates a style to mock it; **caricature** exaggerates features.

blocks.title: Techniques
blocks.md: **Exaggeration**, **understatement**, **mock-seriousness** (a calm tone about an absurd subject), **juxtaposition** (placing contrasting things together), **irony** and **absurd logic**. Satire can be gentle (Horatian) or sharp (Juvenalian). The target and the writer’s tone should be identified.

blocks.caption: Analysing satire in four steps.
blocks.alt: Four boxes: target, technique, tone and effect.

blocks.title: Writing about satire
blocks.md: Identify the **target** (what is criticised), the **technique**, the **tone** and the **effect** on the reader. Ask: is the humour warm or bitter? What would the writer want us to change or think? Always support with quotation.

blocks.title: Mistakes to avoid
blocks.md:
- Treating satire as only funny: it has a serious aim.
- Ignoring the target of the satire.
- Reading ironic statements literally.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Identify the target
blocks.statement: Original extract: ‘The Ministry of Delays announced that the new road would be finished in record time, namely, next to the previous record, which was also next year.’ Identify target and technique.
steps: Target: officials’ unfulfilled promises.
Technique: the ironic name ‘Ministry of Delays’, and the absurd logic of ‘record time’.
Tone: dry, mock-serious.
blocks.answer: Satire of broken promises through irony and absurd logic.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Effect of exaggeration
blocks.statement: Original: ‘The chairman spoke for so long that two of the clocks left the room in protest.’ Comment on the effect.
steps: Hyperbole: clocks cannot leave the room.
Personification makes the clocks critics.
Effect: comic mockery of long-winded speech.
blocks.answer: Humorous criticism through hyperbole and personification.

Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Plan a comparison
blocks.md: Choose 3–4 **points of comparison** that fit the question (for example attitude to authority, narrative voice, language, structure, ending). For each point, note **both texts**: similarity, difference, evidence. Decide which comparison matters most and let it drive your **thesis**.

blocks.title: Structure and language
blocks.md: Prefer an **integrated** structure (point by point) to a block structure (text A then text B). Use comparative language: *similarly, likewise, in contrast, whereas, while, unlike*. Introduce a **counter-argument** (‘It could be argued…’) and respond to it. Make a **judgement** in your conclusion: which text more effectively presents the theme, and why?

blocks.caption: A comparison essay in four steps.
blocks.alt: Four boxes: comparison points, both texts, counter-argument and judgement.

blocks.title: Quality markers
blocks.md: A top essay is **focused** on the question, **analytical** (technique and effect), **evidence-based** with short quotations, **comparative throughout**, **well-organised** and **fluent**. It shows awareness of **context** and **critical approaches** where relevant, without letting them replace close reading.

blocks.title: Pitfalls
blocks.md:
- Treating the two texts separately.
- Retelling plot.
- A conclusion that only repeats the introduction.
- Over-using theory labels without evidence.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Build a thesis
blocks.statement: Question: ‘Compare how two writers present the tension between tradition and change.’ Original texts: A (a poem in which a grandmother keeps an old drum), B (a prose extract in which a son sells his father’s drum). Write a thesis.
steps: Both texts use the drum as a symbol.
A presents tradition as precious and fragile; B shows how economic pressure erodes it.
Thesis: while both writers use the drum as a symbol of heritage, A emphasises preservation and B shows the cost of change.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Write a comparison paragraph
blocks.statement: Write the first point of comparison for the thesis above.
steps: Point: both texts make the drum carry emotional weight.
A: ‘she wipes the drum like a sleeping child’ (imaginary) shows tenderness.
B: ‘it sat in the shop, a price tag on its hide’ shows commodification.
Contrast: affection versus trade.
blocks.answer: Both use the drum as symbol but with different tones.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Original passage: ‘The visitors named our river for their queen and called us a tribe. We kept calling it Mother and calling ourselves by our own names.’ Write a paragraph applying post-colonial criticism.
exercises.model: The passage shows naming as an act of power: the visitors rename the river and label the people, imposing their view. The speaker’s resistance is quiet but strong, as continuing to say ‘Mother’ and ‘our own names’ preserves identity and cultural memory. The contrast between the two names shows the conflict between colonial and local ways of seeing, and the repeated ‘our’ reasserts community.
exercises.rubric: Naming as power (1); resistance (1); language or technique (1); link to theory (1).
exercises.explanation: The passage shows naming as an act of power: the visitors rename the river and label the people, imposing their view. The speaker’s resistance is quiet but strong, as continuing to say ‘Mother’ and ‘our own names’ preserves identity and cultural memory. The contrast between the two names shows the conflict between colonial and local ways of seeing, and the repeated ‘our’ reasserts community.
A founding text of the field.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Original passage: ‘The headmaster spoke; the teachers wrote. When Miss Atem raised a point, the headmaster smiled and continued as before.’ Apply two critical approaches to the passage and compare what each reveals.
exercises.model: A feminist reading sees Miss Atem’s point being ignored with a smile as a sign of how male authority dismisses a woman’s voice. A formalist reading focuses on the sentence structure: the short, parallel clauses (‘spoke’, ‘wrote’) establish a hierarchy, and ‘smiled and continued as before’ gives a calm, understated irony. The feminist approach connects the text to gender and power, the formalist approach shows how the writing creates the effect; together they give a fuller reading.
exercises.explanation: A feminist reading sees Miss Atem’s point being ignored with a smile as a sign of how male authority dismisses a woman’s voice. A formalist reading focuses on the sentence structure: the short, parallel clauses (‘spoke’, ‘wrote’) establish a hierarchy, and ‘smiled and continued as before’ gives a calm, understated irony. The feminist approach connects the text to gender and power, the formalist approach shows how the writing creates the effect; together they give a fuller reading.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Original extract: ‘At the Society for Punctuality the meeting began, as always, an hour after the notice. The secretary apologised for the early start.’ Write a paragraph on how satire works here.
exercises.model: The satire targets those who claim to value punctuality but are always late. The society’s name sets up an expectation that the details contradict. The secretary’s apology for the ‘early’ start is a comic reversal that exaggerates the group’s lateness. The deadpan tone makes the criticism gentle but sharp, inviting us to laugh at hypocrisy.
exercises.rubric: Target (1); irony or reversal (1); tone (1); effect (1).
exercises.explanation: The satire targets those who claim to value punctuality but are always late. The society’s name sets up an expectation that the details contradict. exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Plan (not write in full) an essay on: ‘Compare the presentation of conflict between generations in two extracts.’ Use imaginary extracts: extract X shows a father and daughter arguing over school; extract Y shows a mother silently leaving a room.
exercises.model: Thesis: both extracts show generational conflict, but X is open and verbal while Y is silent and indirect. Para 1: dialogue and tone (X loud and direct; Y silence). Para 2: stage directions or narrative techniques (X reported speech; Y withheld thoughts). Para 3: outcome and message (X reconciliation possible; Y lingering tension). Counter-argument: silence can also be a form of strong speech. Conclusion: judgement that Y’s silence may be more powerful because of what it implies.
exercises.explanation: Thesis: both extracts show generational conflict, but X is open and verbal while Y is silent and indirect. Para 1: dialogue and tone (X loud and direct; Y silence). Para 2: stage directions or narrative techniques (X reported speech; Y withheld thoughts). Para 3: outcome and message (X reconciliation possible; Y lingering tension). Counter-argument: silence can also be a form of strong speech. Conclusion: judgement that Y’s silence may be more powerful because of what it implies.

parts.prompt: Describe the tone of the poem and the effect of the road being ‘empty, patient’ at noon.
parts.model: The tone is quiet, reflective and gently affectionate. The personified road is ‘patient’ and ‘empty’ at noon, suggesting rest and the rhythm of the day, and giving the road a calm presence that contrasts with its busy morning.
parts.explanation: The tone is quiet, reflective and gently affectionate. The personified road is ‘patient’ and ‘empty’ at noon, suggesting rest and the rhythm of the day, and giving the road a calm presence that contrasts with its busy morning.

parts.prompt: How does the poet use the cycle of the day to present the road as part of community life?
parts.model: The poem moves from dawn through noon to evening, so the road follows a daily cycle. At dawn it is busy with feet and songs, at noon it rests, and at night the people’s ‘footprints’ are left for dawn: the road holds the community’s memory and connects generations.
parts.rubric: Structure of the day (1); idea of memory/community (1).
parts.explanation: The poem moves from dawn through noon to evening, so the road follows a daily cycle. At dawn it is busy with feet and songs, at noon it rests, and at night the people’s ‘footprints’ are left for dawn: the road holds the community’s memory and connects generations.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: To what extent is the oral tradition important to African written literature? Refer in general terms to features such as proverbs, storytelling voice and song.
exercises.model: Oral tradition gives many writers forms, rhythms and values: proverbs lend communal wisdom, a storytelling voice invites the audience, and songs add musicality. It shapes structure and humour. But written literature also draws on other influences, such as colonial education, global genres and individual experience. Oral tradition is important but not the only source.
exercises.explanation: Oral tradition gives many writers forms, rhythms and values: proverbs lend communal wisdom, a storytelling voice invites the audience, and songs add musicality. It shapes structure and humour. But written literature also draws on other influences, such as colonial education, global genres and individual experience. Oral tradition is important but not the only source.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: ‘A satirical writer must be bitter to be effective.’ Discuss with reference to techniques of satire.
exercises.model: Bitter satire, with sharp irony, can be powerful and shocking. But gentle satire using humour, understatement and mock-seriousness can also criticise effectively and may persuade readers more easily because it invites them to laugh with the writer. Effectiveness depends on target, tone and audience, so bitterness is not necessary.
exercises.rubric: Argument for bitterness (1); argument against (1); judgement (1).
exercises.explanation: Bitter satire, with sharp irony, can be powerful and shocking. But gentle satire using humour, understatement and mock-seriousness can also criticise effectively and may persuade readers more easily because it invites them to laugh with the writer. Effectiveness depends on target, tone and audience, so bitterness is not necessary.
